svg.aria-label: A spurious bridge: chains either side of an inversion share a diagonal, so a conventional aligner can join them and force an alignment through the inverted sequence, which repeated motifs make possible; scored in bits, the bridge costs far more than explaining the inversion.
svg.text: Aligning through an inversion: a bridge built from repeated motifs
Chains either side of an inversion share a diagonal, so a conventional aligner can join them and align the gap by force.
Repeated motifs let the alignment struggle through, with many indels, although the sequences are not related.
the bridged chr7 record, with 1.9 kb of spurious indels and mismatches,
and B as well: the inverted bases are explained twice, in contradiction
three records: the inversion is reported as such
Schematic. The sequences and the bridge’s counts are illustrative; costs are Parallax’s defaults.
The aligner fills the gap by force
Chains A and C lie on one diagonal, so they chain together and the
1.9 kb between them is aligned. The read there is the inverted
segment, unrelated to the forward reference, but both are built
from the same short motifs, so the alignment finds a path:
44 matches, 10 mismatches, 7 gap columns in this stretch
Chain B is still reported as well, as a secondary + supplementary
record, so the output explains the inverted bases two ways.
The same gap, scored in bits
The inversion costs about 4,600 bits less, so Parallax reports it.
Parallax can bridge too, but must earn it
Parallax aligns seedless gaps of 20–2,000 bp and would try this one.
It keeps the bridge only if that costs less than the alternatives,
on the same scale. With no seeds in the inverted piece at all,
